negative: AI image models cannot reliably render legible modern text (numbers, words, document content, screen text). Never show a notebook page, computer screen, bank statement, or any document with text intended to be read. Frame text-bearing surfaces obliquely, in shadow, partially out of frame, or use the *gesture* of writing/reading (the hand poised over the page, the eye looking at the screen) rather than showing the text itself.

Avoid generic clock or modern device appearances when context calls for specific period (an analog parlour clock in a modern office shot reads wrong). Always specify the clock's setting and era — a sleek modern minimalist clock face, a digital wall clock, etc.

Across consecutive shots showing the same room and characters, reuse the SAME canon tag (e.g. {sarah_meeting} for every shot inside the meeting). Switching from {meeting_room} to {office} to {sarah_office} across consecutive scenes causes the room geometry, furniture, and lighting to invent fresh each time. Pick one canon tag per scene-sequence and stay in it.

Character clothing-state changes (jacket on vs off, top button done vs undone, hair tied vs loose) must be explicit in the prompt for each shot. The base canon describes only the static wardrobe; transitions need per-shot direction. If Sarah's jacket comes off in shot 28, prompt 28 must say 'with her blazer now draped over the chair beside her'.

Every prompt that references a recurring character (Sarah, Mark, or any character defined in canon) MUST use the canon tag (e.g. {sarah} or {mark_meeting}), never the character's name in plain prose. Calling a character by name without the tag bypasses the canon mechanism entirely and lets the model substitute its default-professional prior, causing identity drift across shots. Audit every beat prompt before generation.

Two-character shots overwhelm Flux's attention; combined canon descriptions exceed the model's capacity to honour both characters' specifics. Frame two-character moments as: (a) one character facing camera with the other from behind, (b) no-people detail shots of objects between the absent characters (cups, papers, an empty chair), or (c) tight single-character framings that imply the other through context. Never put both full character canons in one prompt.

Wardrobe details defined in character canon are not reliably honoured prompt-to-prompt; Flux interprets clothing afresh each generation. Every prompt that references a recurring character must explicitly restate the key wardrobe details (the charcoal grey blazer over cream blouse for Sarah; the navy blue suit jacket for Mark) inside the prompt itself, not relying on canon expansion alone. Treat wardrobe as a per-shot directive, identical to clothing-state transitions.

When a single shot fails three reshoots in succession with different failure modes each time (e.g. wrong character, then wrong wardrobe, then wrong setting), the shot is in a high-variance region of the model's output space. Stop reshooting and instead duplicate the closest-acceptable adjacent shot — viewers reading the video at narrative pace will not notice two near-identical adjacent frames, and the rolling-the-dice cost compounds badly. Acceptance > perfection on isolated shots.
